newsitem.title: USA: Dollar ends mixed after see-saw session.
newsitem.headline: Dollar ends mixed after see-saw session.

text.p: The dollar rose against the Japanese yen, but fell to a 49-month low against the British pound during a see-saw trading session Wednesday.
U.S. Treasury Undersecretary Jeffrey Shafer gave the dollar a lift in late U.S. trading by reiterating that the Clinton administration supports a "strong" dollar.

That statement offset a Treasury statement Tuesday that said Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin did not discuss currency rates during a phone call with Japanese Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka, foreign exchange traders said.
Some analysts had interpreted Rubin's comment as a reversal of the Treasury's oft-stated position on the dollar.

"Shafer is well aware of the impact of his statement. The United States and its trading partners are trying to manage the level of the dollar against the yen," said Paul Park, currency trader at Mellon Bank in Pittsburgh.
The dollar ended higher at 111.80 yen, up from 111.47 late Tuesday, and rose to 1.5078 German marks from 1.5072 late Tuesday.

Meanwhile, sterling soared more than one cent to $1.6597, its highest close since October 1992, from $1.6468 late Tuesday. The pound had rallied as high as $1.6628 earlier in the session and also reached a 29-month high against the German mark.
Investors flocked to the pound after a report showed unemployment in Britain fell to 7.2 percent, its lowest point in nearly six years.
A separate report showed Bank of England Governor Eddie George had warned against growing British inflation at a monetary policy meeting on Sept. 23.
Taken together, the reports suggested British officials will soon raise interest rates, even after they raised them on Oct. 30, traders said.
Higher British interest rates would bolster the pound by boosting the relative returns of assets denominated in sterling.

"The hawkish statements from George reinforce the expectation that the U.K. rate hike two weeks ago is not enough and not the last," said Seth Garrett, director of foreign exchange at CS First Boston.
In the United States, the Federal Reserve's policy-making Federal Open Market Committee opted not to change short-term interest rates during its meeting Wednesday.
Few if any market players expected a rate move at the meeting and the dollar failed to move when the panel announced its decision during late U.S. trading.
The dollar drew some support against European currencies in early Wednesday trading when two senior officials of the German central bank hinted that Germany might cut interest rates in the future.

Bundesbank council member Franz-Christoph Zeitler told a banking conference the recent German rate cut cycle had not necessarily ended, while a magazine article quoted fellow council member Olaf Sievert refusing to confirm the easing cycle was over.
In other trade, the dollar rose to 1.2715 Swiss francs from 1.2685. The U.S. currency edged higher to Canadian $1.3335 from C$1.3325.
The Australian dollar rose to $0.7886 from $0.7877. The dollar slipped to 5.0950 French francs from 5.0959.
